sentences.text: Marit was twelve the year the hare turned in the second week of October, which was three weeks early and which nobody at all had been expecting.
She saw it first, from the school bus, which she was extremely pleased about for approximately four hours.
By the evening she understood that being first to see it had put her in the middle of the only argument the village had had in seventeen years.
Because the hare, that year, was wrong.
Everybody could see it was wrong.
The birches still had most of their leaves and the leaves were still half green.
There had not been a frost.

The forecast — and Bjørnstad had had a proper forecast on a phone for about a decade by then, which is important to this — the forecast said mild and wet for the whole of the following fortnight, and then more mild and wet, and the long-range said a late winter.
Her father said the hare had got it wrong and that was all there was to it.
Her mother said the hare had never once got it wrong.

Her father said that a thing that has not got something wrong yet has still only not got it wrong yet, and that he was not lifting two hundred kilos of potatoes in the second week of October on the say-so of a rabbit.
Her mother said it was a hare.
Marit went out to the woodpile, which is what you did in that house when the kitchen got like that.
She split wood for forty minutes, badly, and thought about it.
The thing that bothered her was not that her father might be wrong.
Her father was wrong about plenty of things and said so, eventually, in his own time.
What bothered her was that he had a reason and her mother did not.
Her father could say: here is the forecast, here is where it comes from, here are the satellites, here is a man on the television with a map.
Her mother could say: the hare has never been wrong.

And Marit could see, standing in the cold with the axe, that those two sentences were not the same kind of sentence at all, and that everybody in the village was about to have to choose between them, and that the choosing was going to be based on something other than which one was true.
She went in at nine and her parents were being polite to each other, which was worse.
